enrichment.short_title: Mortgage borrowers fail to set aside 1995 possession order against Paragon Finance
key_facts: Defendants charged their Edgware home to Paragon Finance in 1989; a possession order was made in January 1995 after persistent arrears and was not set aside until this litigation.

On permission-to-appeal hearing before Peter Smith J, new defences were raised: lack of title to sue after securitisation, an implied term limiting exercise of the lender's discretion to vary interest, and an extortionate credit bargain under the Consumer Credit Act 1974.
The loan was not a regulated consumer credit agreement; the defendants had made very limited payments for many years and sought to reopen the possession order and resist enforcement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court hearing of defendants' application for permission to appeal and, if granted, appeal against Barnet County Court orders refusing to set aside a 1995 possession order and permitting enforcement.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted on the set-aside application and new points, but appeal dismissed on all grounds as having no real prospect of success; stay on warrant of possession to be lifted subject to representations on timing.
enrichment.ratio: A mortgagor resisting enforcement of an old possession order cannot succeed on technical title-to-sue, implied-term, or extortionate-credit-bargain arguments where the charge reserved rate-variation and securitisation powers, the agreement was not regulated credit, and there was no evidence the charged rates or undisclosed securitisation policy rendered the bargain extortionate.
legal_issues: Whether Paragon retained title to sue after securitisation of the mortgage
Whether an implied term required fair and good-faith exercise of the lender's discretion to vary interest rates
Whether the mortgage was an extortionate credit bargain despite non-regulation
Whether the possession order could be set aside under repealed CCR Order 37 principles
Whether Article 8 prevented possession and enforcement

enrichment.short_title: Prisoner's judicial review fails over extended licence release date after Home Detention Curfew breach
key_facts: Serving prisoner sentenced to two years' imprisonment was released on Home Detention Curfew, recalled for breach, and was unlawfully at large for 17 days before return to custody.
After later licence revocation, the Secretary of State recalculated the three-quarter release date to 15 December 2003 rather than 28 November 2003 to exclude time at large.
Claimant argued this double-counted the 17-day absence and unlawfully extended his sentence contrary to section 33(3) and Article 5.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of the Secretary of State's recalculation of licence release and sentence expiry dates.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review refused; permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal refused; no costs order against the claimant.
enrichment.ratio: Time spent unlawfully at large after recall from Home Detention Curfew is excluded from sentence served under section 49(2) of the Prison Act 1952, with consequential postponement of automatic conditional release, licence expiry, and sentence expiry dates; this is not double counting or unlawful extension of the court-imposed term.
legal_issues: Effect of unlawfully-at-large time on three-quarter licence release under section 33(3) CJA 1991
Interaction between sections 38A and 49(2) and Prison Service Orders on HDC recall
Whether recalculation breached Article 5 ECHR
Whether the Secretary of State should exercise discretion to count UAL time towards sentence

enrichment.short_title: Green Belt gypsy caravan permission quashed where children's schooling held not 'very special circumstances'
key_facts: Mrs Draper, a gypsy, occupied an unauthorised caravan site in the Green Belt at Runwell, Essex; the Secretary of State allowed her appeal and granted conditional retention permission.
The sole very special circumstance relied on was that her two primary-school-age children were settled at a local school within walking distance.
The family had previously occupied an authorised gypsy pitch and chose to move to the unauthorised site; harm to the Green Belt was accepted as limited but inappropriate development in principle.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 statutory challenge by Chelmsford Borough Council to quash the Secretary of State's planning appeal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Application succeeded on ground 2; decision quashed; Secretary of State ordered to pay costs summarily assessed at £4,590.
enrichment.ratio: Under PPG2, very special circumstances must be circumstances objectively capable of being described as 'very special', not merely factors the decision-maker weighs heavily; commonplace educational needs of two young children at a local school cannot reasonably satisfy that test even where further Green Belt harm is limited.
legal_issues: Whether the decision letter conflated harm in principle with limited visual harm under PPG2 paragraph 3.2
Whether ordinary children's educational needs could amount to very special circumstances
Whether a decision-maker may treat any outweighing factor as very special circumstances
Whether reference to general suitability of the area for gypsy occupation created a bad precedent

enrichment.short_title: Rival developer fails to quash Brighouse retail planning permission for defective EIA screening

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Environmental Impact Assessment) (England and Wales) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Called-in planning permission was granted in November 2002 for a major retail and leisure redevelopment on a 3.777 ha former mill site in Brighouse after a public inquiry.

Claimant Younger Homes, a later land purchaser seeking residential development, challenged the grant for failure to make a valid EIA screening direction, relying on alleged defects in Calderdale MBC's 1999 screening opinion.
Officer Mr Raper concluded redevelopment was not EIA development; the opinion was handwritten, not sent to the applicant, and not placed on the planning register, though it was on the file.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to the Secretary of State's grant of planning permission on EIA screening and delegation grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; Secretary of State and Calderdale MBC awarded costs; leave to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: A lawfully adopted screening opinion by an authorised planning officer can satisfy regulation 8 even if informally recorded; procedural failures to notify the applicant or register the opinion do not vitiate the Secretary of State's decision where the obligation to consider EIA necessity was fulfilled and the challenger suffered no substantial prejudice.

Whether the screening opinion unlawfully relied on a future traffic impact assessment instead of EIA criteria
Whether contamination and outline-application uncertainties required EIA
Whether failure to send or register the screening opinion invalidated planning permission
Whether an unlawful screening opinion could be relied on in a section 288 challenge without prior JR

enrichment.short_title: PCS Union VAT appeal partly succeeds over attribution of subscription income to zero-rated magazines
key_facts: PCS Union received member subscriptions funding a package of benefits including zero-rated union magazines with no separate cover price.
Customs assessed additional VAT for 1998-1999 accounting periods using a cost-based attribution of subscription value to magazine supplies.
Tribunal upheld assessments; union appealed, arguing market value (£1.80 per copy) should be used and that the cost method wrongly excluded network employment overheads.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal from VAT and Duties Tribunal decision upholding Customs' section 73 best-judgment assessments.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; tribunal decision set aside and remitted for fresh hearing on overheads/staff-cost attribution; market-value method rejected on the evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 19(4) VATA 1994 neither market-value nor cost attribution is mandatory in all cases; but where Customs used a cost method excluding £7.5m of network employment overheads without inquiry, despite audited accounts indicating broader attributable costs, that was an error of law warranting remission.

Whether the Commissioners' cost-based apportionment lawfully included network administration employment costs

enrichment.short_title: Attorney General may refer unduly lenient failure to make confiscation orders after procedural defects
key_facts: In two unrelated fraud cases, Crown Court judges declined to embark on confiscation hearings, relying on since-overruled Court of Appeal decisions in Palmer and Pisciotto on defective postponement or notice.
Substantial benefit figures were alleged (£2m in Smith/Bradley; £500,000 in Cunningham/Graver/Flowers).
Attorney General sought references under section 36 as unduly lenient sentencing for failure to make confiscation orders.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's references to the Court of Appeal under section 36 CJA 1988 following Crown Court refusals to conduct confiscation proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: References allowed; court held it had jurisdiction to review and make appropriate confiscation orders after factual hearing; discretion exercised to permit Cunningham reference despite delay.
enrichment.ratio: A Crown Court decision declining jurisdiction to make a confiscation order amounts to 'making no order' on the application and is itself a sentence amenable to Attorney General reference as unduly lenient; the Court of Appeal may then exercise the confiscation power the Crown Court wrongly thought unavailable.

enrichment.short_title: Wall Street Journal libel appeal: Chase level-3 meaning restored; hearsay evidence admissible on Reynolds privilege
key_facts: Jameel family companies sued over a February 2002 Wall Street Journal Europe article reporting SAMA monitoring of Saudi businessmen's bank accounts for potential terrorist ties.

At pre-trial review Eady J ruled the words bore at least Chase tier-2 meaning ('reasonable grounds to suspect') and admitted SAMA/bank hearsay statements to disprove monitoring despite no plea of justification.
Defendant relied on Reynolds qualified privilege; trial was listed for December 2003.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Defendant's interlocutory appeal against Eady J's rulings on meaning and admissibility of hearsay evidence in libel proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part on meaning (lesser Chase tier-3 'grounds for investigation' meaning not excluded from jury); appeal dismissed on hearsay admissibility.
enrichment.ratio: A judge should not delimit defamatory meaning so as to exclude Chase tier-3 imputations where the article's misconduct underlying monitoring is ambiguous; hearsay denying account monitoring may be admitted to challenge journalists' account of source conversations without determining truth for Reynolds privilege purposes.
legal_issues: Whether the article was capable of bearing only tier-2 'reasonable grounds to suspect' meaning
Distinction between Chase tier-2 and tier-3 defamatory meanings in terrorism-funding context

enrichment.short_title: Exclusive haulage contract breached when Nedlloyd merged operations and ended separate transport requirements
key_facts: CEL held exclusive three-year contract from July 1996 to provide all Nedlloyd Lines UK's road haulage, including a dedicated fleet of at least 35 vehicles.
At end of 1996 Nedlloyd merged with P & O; from May 1997 merged haulage operations meant NLL no longer had separately identifiable transport requirements and CEL lost exclusive access to most work.
CEL continued some merged-group work but owner-driver and subcontractor flows fell sharply, reducing profitability.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against Andrew Smith J's judgment finding breach of contract and awarding damages with inquiry as to cash-flow loss.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; implied-term breach upheld; costs order against appellant with £35,000 on account.
enrichment.ratio: Where a contract grants exclusive rights to supply all of a company's defined haulage requirements for a fixed term, there is an implied obligation (Stirling v Maitland) that the customer will not voluntarily destroy the continuing state of affairs in which those requirements exist; voluntary merger eliminating discrete business needs is a breach.
legal_issues: Whether exclusive haulage contract implied a term that Nedlloyd would maintain separate transport requirements
Distinction from agency cases such as Luxor v Cooper where principals may dispose of business freely
Whether clause 4(a)(ii) liquidated damages for unused dedicated vehicles excluded damages for loss of wider work
Construction of exclusive supply contract against long prior exclusive joint-venture background
